title: PRIVACY HAS MORE THAN ONE ENEMY
subtitle: CRYPTOGRAPHY CAN HIDE THE TRANSACTION. YOU CAN STILL REVEAL YOURSELF.

blocks.text: A PRIVATE PROTOCOL CAN PROTECT THE DATA IT CONTROLS. IT CANNOT PROTECT INFORMATION YOU HAND OUT SOMEWHERE ELSE.
CRYPTOGRAPHY HAS A BORDER.

Shielded protocols can radically reduce what a public ledger exposes. But practical financial privacy is a system, not a switch. The blockchain is one component. The wallet is another. The network connection, exchange, recipient, viewing keys, screenshots, transaction IDs and things a user says publicly all sit outside or around the cryptographic core.
That distinction matters because a protocol can work exactly as designed while privacy still fails somewhere else.
01 // THE PROTOCOL ONLY OWNS ITS LAYER

Inside Orchard, commitments and zero-knowledge proofs allow hidden note information to participate in consensus without being published as ordinary transparent payment data. That gives the protocol strong tools for ledger privacy. But Orchard does not control what an exchange records before a withdrawal, what a merchant knows after a purchase or what a user posts afterward.

Privacy therefore needs a threat model. Are you trying to hide payment details from the public ledger? From a network observer? From the counterparty? From a custodian that already knows your identity? Different observers see different surfaces.
02 // DISCLOSURE CAN RECREATE A LINK

Zcash's own privacy recommendations warn against leaking transaction IDs, amounts and counterparty information because these can be used to create linkages. This is not merely a warning for transparent addresses. External metadata can supply context around shielded activity too.

A private transaction followed by a public receipt is no longer private from everyone who sees that receipt. A shielded payment discussed with an identified counterparty is not anonymous to that counterparty. A transaction ID handed to a support desk becomes information available to that service. Privacy depends on who knows what, not on whether one technology carries the word private.
THE CHAIN CAN FORGET THE DETAILS YOU NEVER PUT ON IT. THE PEOPLE YOU TELL DO NOT HAVE TO.
03 // VIEWING KEYS ARE DELIBERATE DISCLOSURE

Zcash includes viewing-key mechanisms precisely because privacy and selective disclosure are different from absolute secrecy. The privacy guidance warns users not to share viewing keys without understanding the consequences. Giving another party viewing capability changes who can inspect the associated information even though the underlying shielded protocol remains unchanged.
This is an important design idea: privacy can be selective. But selective disclosure only works when the user understands which capability is being shared and with whom.
04 // BOUNDARIES CAN MAKE VALUES PUBLIC

Some leakage is not accidental behavior at all; it is defined by the protocol boundary. ZIP 224 states that spending funds residing in the Orchard pool to a non-Orchard address reveals the value of that transaction. Orchard-to-Orchard activity and movement across the Orchard boundary therefore do not have identical privacy properties.
That is why 'shielded' should never be interpreted as a promise that every surrounding fact remains hidden in every transaction shape. The exact path matters.
05 // NETWORK PRIVACY IS ANOTHER PROBLEM

The Zcash peer-to-peer network uses IP connections and does not itself obfuscate user IP addresses. Zcash documentation warns that a unique IP address can let a network observer correlate transactions with each other or with other traffic. Again, this is outside the ledger-level protection provided by a shielded proof.
The lesson is not that shielded cryptography failed. The lesson is that network anonymity and transaction confidentiality are separate engineering problems.
06 // PRIVACY FAILS BY COMPOSITION

A user may have excellent ledger privacy and poor network privacy. Strong network privacy and a fully identified exchange account. A private payment followed by a public screenshot. A shielded balance with a viewing key shared too broadly. Each component can be understood separately, but the final privacy outcome comes from how they compose.

This is why operational privacy matters. It is not a substitute for cryptography. It is what stops behavior and surrounding infrastructure from undoing protections the cryptography successfully provided.
PRIVACY IS NOT ONE WALL. IT IS A SERIES OF DOORS. CRYPTOGRAPHY CAN LOCK SOME OF THEM. YOU STILL HAVE TO NOTICE THE REST.
07 // ASK WHO STILL KNOWS

After any private payment, ask a simple sequence of questions. What did the public ledger learn? What did the network learn? What did the wallet provider or remote server learn? What did the exchange already know? What did the recipient learn? What did I reveal afterward?
That produces a more accurate picture than asking whether the transaction was simply private or not.

The proof can protect what you keep inside the proof. Privacy begins to break where the rest of your life touches it.
